title: Work and Careers
learningObjectives: Understand vocabulary related to jobs, workplaces, and career paths
Read about job applications and interviews
Learn phrases for discussing skills and experience
Practice understanding workplace situations and challenges

sections.title: Choosing a Career
sections.content: Work takes up a large part of adult life, so choosing the right career matters. People consider salary, working hours, and whether a job matches their skills and interests. This lesson explores common vocabulary and situations related to careers and the workplace.

sections.title: Looking for a Job
sections.content:
When searching for work, people check <job listings> on websites or in newspapers. They send a <CV> (or <resume>) and a <cover letter> to apply.

If the employer is interested, they invite the candidate to an <interview>. During the interview, the candidate talks about their <skills>, <experience>, and <qualifications>.

sections.title: At the Workplace
sections.content:
Once hired, an employee has a <job title>, works under a <manager> or <supervisor>, and receives a <salary>. Some people work <full-time>, while others prefer <part-time> hours.

Common workplace terms include <deadline> (the date work must be finished), <colleague> (a person you work with), and <promotion> (moving to a higher position).

sections.title: Career Conversations
sections.content:
Example 1: JOB INTERVIEW - <Tell me about your previous work experience.>

Example 2: DISCUSSING SKILLS - <I'm good at working in a team and solving problems.>

Example 3: ASKING ABOUT SALARY - <What is the salary range for this position?>

sections.title: Workplace Challenges
sections.content:
Not every day at work is easy. People sometimes deal with <stress>, tight <deadlines>, or disagreements with colleagues. Learning to <manage your time> and <communicate clearly> helps solve many problems.

If someone is unhappy with their job, they might look for a <career change> or ask for <feedback> from their manager to improve.

sections.title: Workplace Problem Solving
sections.content:
Example 1: MISSED DEADLINE - <A: I'm sorry, I couldn't finish the report on time.
B: Let's talk about how to manage your workload better.>

Example 2: ASKING FOR HELP - <A: Could you help me with this project? I'm a bit stuck.
B: Of course, let's go through it together.>

Example 3: REQUESTING TIME OFF - <A: Could I take next Friday off?
B: Sure, just send me a request in advance.>

sections.title: Career Growth
sections.content:
Many people want to grow professionally. They take <training courses>, learn new <skills>, or aim for a <promotion>. Networking, or building relationships with other professionals, can also open new opportunities.

Setting clear <career goals> helps people decide what steps to take next, whether that means changing jobs, gaining certifications, or starting their own business.

sections.title: Career Tips
sections.content:
Remember these key points: Prepare well before a job interview by researching the company. Highlight your skills and experience clearly. Communicate professionally with colleagues and managers.

Don't be afraid to ask for feedback or set new career goals. A career is a long journey, so keep learning along the way!

keyVocabulary.definition: A document listing your work experience and skills
keyVocabulary.example: Please attach your resume to the email.

keyVocabulary.definition: A formal meeting to discuss a job application
keyVocabulary.example: My interview is scheduled for Monday morning.

keyVocabulary.definition: The date by which something must be finished
keyVocabulary.example: We need to meet the deadline on Friday.
My colleague helped me finish the report.

keyVocabulary.definition: A move to a higher position at work
keyVocabulary.example: She got a promotion after two years.

keyVocabulary.definition: A skill or achievement that makes someone suitable for a job
keyVocabulary.example: This job requires a degree in marketing as a qualification.

grammarPoints.explanation: Use the present perfect (<have/has> + past participle) to talk about work experience that connects to now.
examples: I have worked in marketing for three years.
commonMistakes: Using the past simple instead of present perfect for ongoing experience

grammarPoints.explanation: Use <be good at> + noun or -ing verb to describe skills.
examples: She is good at solving problems.
commonMistakes: Using the base verb instead of -ing after "good at"
